name: Shelf — the agent skills ecosystem as a browsable library
one_liner: A free, no-signup shelf view of every public agent skill — thousands of SKILL.md files rendered as spines on a library shelf, sorted by installs, where pulling one out shows what it actually tells your agent to do and which shell, network and file powers it asks for.
problem: For anyone running `npx skills add`, the agent-skills ecosystem is now thousands of entries across skills.sh, skillsdirectory.com, agenticskills.io and linkly.ai, all presented as the same ranked list of cards. There is no way to see the shape of the ecosystem — what people actually install, what a skill really contains, how many of them quietly ask for shell access. Today you either scroll a leaderboard or clone a repo and read Markdown. Shelf makes the whole corpus browsable in one screen and makes one skill legible in one click.
target_customer: Developers using Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Devin who install skills — they hang out on X, in r/ClaudeAI, and in the skills directories themselves. Secondary: people who build and publish skills and want to see where theirs sits on the shelf.
why_now: The ecosystem went from nothing to thousands of public skills in under a year (one directory reports 5,200+ community skills as of April 2026; the top skill, security-review, shows 18,189 installs on skills.sh as of 2026-10-15). skills.sh now documents a JSON API — /api/v1/skills for the paginated leaderboard with install counts, /api/v1/skills/{source}/{skill} returning full file contents including SKILL.md, and /api/v1/skills/audit/{source}/{skill} for security findings. A corpus this size with install telemetry and full text did not exist six months ago. The bookmark that triggered it: @jakubkrehel's /teardown skill shipped via `npx skills add` picked up 6,000 likes in a day, which is the ecosystem's distribution surface working in public.
comparables: skills.sh (www.skills.sh) — the canonical registry and leaderboard, but a ranked list of cards; its API also appears to require auth for v1, so Shelf must snapshot rather than call live. skillsdirectory.com — security grades and findings per skill behind an API key, one skill at a time. agenticskills.io — curated catalog that explicitly refuses to show install counts. linkly.ai/skills and skillselion.com/leaderboard — daily top-100 lists aggregated across skills.sh, ClawHub and Tencent SkillHub. Harmonic's skill-scan-io and Plastikelectrik/skill-auditor — open-source scanners for one skill or directory. Nobody has rendered the corpus itself as a single browsable object, and nobody shows ecosystem-wide capability distribution (what fraction of skills request shell, network, credentials). That is the gap and it is a presentation gap, exactly the kind the taste file's 'research papers as a shelf of books' occupies. Differs from the library's Skillscope, which X-rays one skill you are about to install for safety; Shelf is a browsable corpus view of all of them with a different audience moment — discovery, not pre-install vetting.
risks: 1. The skills.sh v1 API appears to require authentication (reports of 401 without credentials), so the corpus may have to be assembled from GitHub repos instead — more scraping work and weaker install-count data, which is the thing that makes the shelf interesting. 2. One-time-toy risk: people look at the pretty shelf once and never return; the return reason has to be real (weekly 'what's new on the shelf' diff, or genuinely better discovery than the leaderboards). 3. Four directories already compete on discovery and one of them could ship a nicer view in an afternoon; Shelf's only defence is that it is free, open source, and the only one showing the whole corpus at once.
build_plan: Stack: a build-time Node script + a static Next.js or plain-Vite site on Vercel, no backend, no runtime API calls. Steps: (1) snapshot the corpus — hit skills.sh /api/v1/skills paginated for the leaderboard (name, source, installs, installUrl) and /api/v1/skills/{source}/{skill} for files including SKILL.md; fall back to the GitHub API over the known skill repos if auth blocks the v1 endpoints, and cache everything to a single JSON file committed to the repo. (2) Static-analyse each SKILL.md locally with regex + a tiny heuristic pass: does it reference shell/bash execution, network fetch, credentials/env, filesystem writes? Store four booleans and the matching line numbers — no model call needed, so cost is zero. (3) Render the shelf: CSS-only book spines, spine height scaled to log(installs), spine colour by capability profile (green = text only, amber = network, red = shell), grouped into shelves by category. (4) Click a spine → the book opens: title, author/repo, install count, the `npx skills add` command with a copy button, the rendered SKILL.md, and the highlighted capability lines. (5) One filter row: search, capability toggles, and a 'sort by installs / newest / most shell-happy' control. (6) A single shareable stat strip at the top: 'N skills · M total installs · X% ask for shell'. Cut: live API calls, auth, user accounts, any LLM in the loop, writing to any registry, and mobile-perfect layout.
launch_post:
I pulled every public agent skill into one page and rendered them as a library shelf.

Spine height = installs. Spine colour = what the skill asks for (green: text only, red: shell access).

Pull one out to read its SKILL.md with the risky lines highlighted.

Free, no signup, open source:
reasoning: Beat the other build candidates because the dependency is a real public corpus rather than a paid image model, it costs nothing to run (static site, regex analysis, zero inference), it matches the taste file's favourite pattern exactly — public data, one clever presentation, a screenshot that explains itself — and it is comfortably a weekend for someone fluent in TypeScript and static sites. It shares no audience or workflow with the venture: Shelf is a free browsable dataset for agent developers, Receipts is paid evidence infrastructure for medical billing managers.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Receipts — proof-of-submission evidence vault for payer-portal work (from the Pomerado launch + the browser-agent reliability thread). KEPT: researched competitors (Skyvern $29-149/mo, Pomerado free/$50/mo, Klivira, ASSERTUS, Steel, Blue Prism/AA audit docs) and found all of them sell execution reliability or admin audit, none sells vendor-neutral transaction-level proof to a non-developer buyer. Non-software buyer, as required.
2. Agent attribution & undo for shared mailboxes/calendars (from @sriramk's "need an agent watching over all my personal agents"). DROPPED: Microsoft Agent 365 + Purview and Google Workspace Studio are shipping agent identity and audit natively in 2026, so the gap closes against two incumbents who own the data; also uncomfortably close to Holdroom and Driftwatch already in the library.
3. Consent-and-compliance layer for Meta Marketing Messages blasts (from the Blueberry Social Broadcasts post). DROPPED: research showed opt-in consent is enforced by Meta itself and is the platform's own gate, not a product; the buyer is a growth marketer who buys ROAS, not a compliance tool, so there is no clear budget owner.
4. Portal-change regression monitor sold to RPA teams (variant of #1 aimed at developers). DROPPED as a thin variation — same workflow as Receipts but sold to the vendor whose bot broke, which is the buyer least motivated to pay, and it overlaps Driftwatch in the library.

BUILD
1. Shelf — the whole public agent-skills corpus rendered as a browsable library shelf with install-scaled spines and capability colouring (from @jakubkrehel's /teardown skill shipping via npx skills add). KEPT: corpus is real and large (5,200+ skills reported; 18,189 installs on the top skill), skills.sh documents the data shape, zero inference cost, matches the taste file's shelf-of-papers entry.
2. URL → exploded UI teardown poster (from the same /teardown bookmark + @Mappletons on interface abstraction levels). DROPPED: Fleck, UXLens and urltodesign.md already cover annotated URL critique, and research found no way to get genuinely layered output from an image model — the result would be a raster picture pretending to be a diagram.
3. Photo → annotated exploded parts diagram. DROPPED as a near-repeat of Partsy and Flatpack already in the library, and Nano Banana Pro has no free API tier ($0.134 per 1K image), which breaks the "free to try, no signup" rule the taste file insists on.
4. Agent-skill capability scanner as a one-input web page. DROPPED: that is Skillscope, already in the library, and Harmonic's skill-scan-io plus two open-source auditors already do it free.
5. Live ecosystem leaderboard of skills by installs. DROPPED: skillselion.com, linkly.ai and skills.sh all already publish exactly this as ranked lists — Shelf only survives because it is a different presentation of the corpus, not another leaderboard.
research_notes:
Budget used: 3 reading calls, 12 venture calls, 7 build calls (22 of 22). No images could be seen; every bookmark with video-only media was judged on its text plus a summary call where the text was too thin.

READING (3): Pomerado (YC F26) — confirmed it mints a typed API/MCP integration from a plain-language task by exploring the site with Chromium, MIT core, cloud free tier 100 calls/day and $50/mo premium, and that its differentiator is auto-repair when a site changes. supermemory learner-1 — confirmed it is external memory for agents with published pricing ($0/$19/$100/$399), which killed a candidate about "memory for ops teams" before it cost any venture budget. Blueberry Social Broadcasts — the summary showed Meta Marketing Messages require explicit opt-in and the platform enforces it, which is what sank that venture candidate. (Cursor Agent SDK was also summarised and treated as context on the crowded agent-dev-tools market rather than as a candidate source.)

VENTURE (12): searched for insurance-portal and freight-portal automation startups, for agent attribution/audit products, and for proof-of-submission products in healthcare, permits and claims. The pivotal findings: (a) a direct comparison showing Skyvern ($29/$149/mo) and Pomerado Cloud sell adaptation to UI change, while Blue Prism and Automation Anywhere documentation shows session and admin audit logs but no automatic capture of the portal's returned receipt correlated to a business item — this is what defined the gap and turned a vague "monitor your browser agents" idea into Receipts; (b) Klivira advertises screenshot evidence of prior-auth confirmations and ASSERTUS centralises EDI acknowledgment receipts, which narrowed the wedge to *vendor-neutral* evidence spanning human and bot submissions; (c) timely-filing (CO-29) proof is a documented, named pain with a recognised evidence hierarchy, but no source isolates the dollars lost specifically to missing proof — so market_pull and pain were capped at 7 and the validation test was rewritten to target exactly that number; (d) a market call returned a ~$840M US denial-management software estimate and ~$6-8B billing-outsourcing services, both labelled as estimates in the brief; (e) the attribution candidate was dropped after a summary showed Microsoft Agent 365/Purview and Google Workspace Studio already building agent identity and auditability. A freight/retail-portal search was run as the alternative non-software buyer and returned no defensible benchmarks, which is why healthcare won the slot.

BUILD (7): confirmed the skills corpus is real and large (5,200+ community skills reported April 2026; security-review at 18,189 installs on skills.sh as of 2026-10-15) and mapped the data access precisely — skills.sh documents /api/v1/skills (leaderboard with install counts), /api/v1/skills/{source}/{skill} (returns files including full SKILL.md) and an audit endpoint, but v1 appears to require authentication with 401s reported for anonymous calls, so the build plan was changed to a committed static snapshot with a GitHub-API fallback and buildability was scored 7 rather than 8. Checked competing directories (skillselion, linkly.ai, agenticskills.io, skillsdirectory.com) and found all present ranked card lists and none shows the corpus as one object or ecosystem-wide capability distribution — that confirmed the presentation gap. Separately checked the teardown-illustration ideas: Nano Banana Pro has no free API tier for image generation (~$0.134 per 1K image, $0.24 at 4K) and cannot emit layered/semantic SVG, and SeeCode, Fleck, UXLens and ScreenDesc already cover the adjacent ground — which is why those candidates were dropped rather than reshaped, and why the capability analysis in Shelf is regex-based with no model in the loop.
prototype_summary: Shelf is a browsable CSS library of 14 agent skills whose spine height maps to installs and colour to capability, with click-to-open two-page SKILL.md spreads that highlight risky lines.
